title: Anthropic’s IPO Triumph
summary: Anthropic pulled it off. The biggest pure-play AI company out there, maker of the Claude line of AI models, went public on Thursday, with its shares jumping as much as 39% above its IPO price. The stock settled back a bit to close at $97.17, up 17% from its IPO price. That gave it a market capitalization of $1.76 trillion, assuming you include all options, restricted stock units and convertible notes that might one day become shares. Not bad for a company that’s just five years old.What makes the IPO even more notable is that it occurred despite months of investor jitters about the cost of AI development. Partly as a result of those jitters, we’ve had a very choppy market that has stalled IPO plans by a slew of other companies—including data center developers SB Energy and Nscale that filed publicly over the summer. Notably, SB Energy on Thursday updated its IPO filing for the first time since late September, suggesting it was still hoping to go public, while Nscale updated its filing a week ago also for the first time since September. But Anthropic’s success doesn’t mean the IPO market has opened up. “I don't think this opens the floodgates unless you look like Anthropic,” Lise Buyer, managing partner of Class V Group, said on a subscriber video discussion convened by The Information.
title_es: IPO de Anthropic abre mercado a pesar de incertidumbre de costos
bajada: El debut en bolsa de Anthropic desafió meses de jitters inversores sobre costos de desarrollo de IA, con sus acciones subiendo 17% desde el precio IPO. El éxito sugiere que solo empresas de calibre Anthropic lograrán acceso al mercado en el corto plazo.
bajada_en: Anthropic's public debut defied months of investor concerns about AI development costs, with shares jumping 17% from IPO price. The success suggests that only companies of Anthropic's caliber will gain near-term market access.

title: LLM Complexity: Towards a Computational Complexity View of Large Language Model Inference
summary:
arXiv:2611.24943v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Computational complexity theory offers a principled framework for characterizing the efficiency of computational problems, and Large Language Models (LLMs) can similarly be viewed as computational systems executing a structured process of input, inference-time compute, and output. In this context, the number of generated tokens emerges as a natural and directly observable proxy for inference-time compute. However, we show that the tempting analogy between LLM token length and classical time complexity does not hold. We disprove the hypothesis that inference-time token usage aligns monotonically with classical time complexity, demonstrating a fundamental divergence grounded in how LLMs actually allocate computation during inference. To this end, we introduce LLM Complexity, a new metric designed to quantify problem complexity from the perspective of LLMs by characterizing the area bounded above by the accuracy-token curve. We find that diverse LLMs induce highly consistent task rankings under LLM Complexity, indicating that the metric captures stable notions of difficulty across models. We leverage this property to construct an easy-to-hard curriculum for supervised fine-tuning, which improves accuracy while reducing token consumption. Finally, we demonstrate that LLM Complexity generalizes to real-world tasks, producing more stable cross-model correlations than human-annotated difficulty labels.
title_es: Proponen teoría de complejidad computacional para inferencia en LLMs
bajada: Un paper arXiv introduce 'LLM Complexity', métrica para cuantificar dificultad de problemas desde la perspectiva de LLMs más allá de tokens. Demuestra inconsistencias entre complejidad clásica y cómo LLMs asignan computación.
bajada_en: An arXiv paper introduces 'LLM Complexity', a metric to quantify problem difficulty from LLMs' perspective beyond token count. It reveals inconsistencies between classical complexity and how LLMs allocate computation.
